the study of the Pfeiffer effect with the aid of chiral solvatochromic probes and the use of chiral solutes as an environment substance.
the development of a new method for the resolution of a racemic complex, which is based on the Pfeiffer effect with an environment substance.
the Pfeiffer effect in the chiral equilibrium of a racemate in water and with its application to the resolution of the racemate.

the chiral equilibrium shift of [Cr( ox)2(phen) ]− toward its (+) enantiomer was caused by the combined action of the following two factors: (i) the electrostatic interactions between the complex anion and the cation, and (ii) the hydrophobic interactions between the phenanthroline ligand and the cation.

, when the complex and the environment substance (quininium or quinidinium cation) are in the same chiral configuration, the chiral equilibrium of the complex is shifted toward the (+) or (−) enantiomer, while the opposite is observed when the complex and environment substance are in the opposite configuration.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Pfeiffer effect can be applied to the racemization system of [Cr(phen)(ox)2]− in water.

the chiral equilibrium of the [Cr(ox)(phen)2]+ ion was found to be shifted toward its (+) and (−) enantiomer by the addition of (+) and (–) quinine or quinidine hydrochloride to the solution in water.

the Pfeiffer effect is a powerful tool for the chiral equilibrium shift of the [Cr(ox)]3− system in water, and the chiral shift can be attained by using not only a chiral ligand but also a chiral salt as an environment substance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the chiral equilibrium of a complex can be displaced greatly by a chiral environment substance.
a racemic complex in a water environment can be converted to a chiral form by the addition of an environment substance that has a chiral center and a π-π stacking ability.

the Pfeiffer effect can be utilized to attain a significant equilibrium shift in a racemate of a chiral complex by using a chiral environment substance, and that the extent of the equilibrium shift can be controlled by the amount of environment substance added to water.
